Tomato___Late_blight.Cause: Late blight is caused by the oomycete (a fungus-like organism) Phytophthora infestans. In wet conditions, late blight spreads very quickly across foliage and tubers/fruits and can cause the death of an entire plant in 7 to 10 days, if untreated. The pathogen can also survive between seasons and can spread through infected seed tubers/tomato seedlings, or any infected plant material that remains after harvest (like potato-waste dumps).
Tomato___Late_blight.Prevention: Practice crop rotation (avoid planting tomato/potato back-to-back), Ensure proper spacing for good air circulation, Avoid overhead irrigation / wet foliage, Remove and destroy infected plant debris, Avoid working in fields when plants are wet, Use resistant or tolerant varieties if available
Tomato___Late_blight.Treatment: Remove and burn infected leaves and plants immediately, Apply disease-specific fungicides early and repeat as per disease progression, Monitor fields frequently during weather favorable for disease (cool + humid)
Tomato___Late_blight.Pesticide: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, Copper oxychloride / Copper hydroxide, Metalaxyl + Mancozeb, Dimethomorph + Mancozeb, Fluopicolide + Propamocarb
Tomato___Late_blight.Organic solution: Neem Oil Spray, Trichoderma spp. (biofungicide), Baking Soda + Water Spray, Garlic Extract Spray, Organic compost tea spray, Mulching & Soil Solarization

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.Cause:
Tomato leaf mold is caused by a fungal pathogen : Passalora fulva (syn. Cladosporium fulvum)
The fungus develops rapidly under high humidity, poor air circulation, and moderate temperatures, especially in greenhouses and protected cultivation.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.Prevention: Use disease-free and certified seedlings, Grow resistant or tolerant tomato varieties, Maintain proper spacing between plants, Ensure good ventilation (especially in polyhouses), Avoid overhead irrigation, Remove and destroy infected leaves and plant debris, Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, Practice crop rotation
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.Treatment: Remove infected leaves at early stages, Improve air circulation and reduce moisture, Apply recommended fungicides at proper intervals, Monitor crop regularly, especially during humid weather
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.Pesticide: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, Copper oxychloride, Hexaconazole, Propiconazole, Azoxystrobin
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Trichoderma viride / Trichoderma harzianum, Garlic extract spray, Baking soda solution, Compost tea spray, Proper ventilation & sanitation

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.Cause:
Septoria leaf spot of tomato is caused by a fungal pathogen : Septoria lycopersici
The fungus survives on infected crop debris and spreads through rain splash, irrigation water, tools, and workers, especially under warm and humid conditions.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.Prevention: Use disease-free and certified seeds/seedlings, Practice crop rotation with non-host crops, Maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation, Avoid overhead irrigation, Remove and destroy infected plant debris, Use mulching to reduce soil splash, Maintain good field sanitation, Avoid working in wet fields
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.Treatment: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves, Improve field aeration and reduce leaf wetness, Apply recommended fungicides at early stages, Monitor disease progression regularly during humid weather
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.Pesticide: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, Copper oxychloride, Carbendazim, Propiconazole, Azoxystrobin
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Trichoderma viride / Trichoderma harzianum, Garlic or ginger extract spray, Compost tea spray, Mulching with straw or plastic, Regular removal of infected leaves

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.Cause:
Two-spotted spider mite infestation in tomato is caused by an insect pest : Tetranychus urticae (two-spotted spider mite)
The pest thrives in hot, dry weather and multiplies rapidly, feeding on plant sap from the underside of leaves.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.Prevention: Use healthy, pest-free seedlings, Maintain proper field sanitation, Avoid excessive use of nitrogen fertilizers, Maintain adequate irrigation to reduce plant stress, Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves, Encourage natural predators (lady beetles, predatory mites), Avoid unnecessary pesticide sprays that kill beneficial insects
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.Treatment: Spray recommended acaricides at early infestation stage, Repeat sprays if infestation persists, Focus spray on underside of leaves, Monitor crop regularly during hot and dry conditions
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.Pesticide: Abamectin, Spiromesifen, Propargite, Fenazaquin, Dicofol, Bifenazate
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Soap solution / Insecticidal soap, Garlic-chili extract spray, Predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis), Sulfur-based spray, Maintain field humidity

Tomato___Target_Spot.Cause:
Target spot of tomato is caused by a fungal pathogen : Corynespora cassiicola
The fungus survives on infected plant debris and spreads through air-borne spores, especially under warm, humid conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.Prevention: Use disease-free and certified seedlings, Practice crop rotation with non-host crops, Maintain proper plant spacing for good air circulation, Avoid overhead irrigation, Remove and destroy infected plant debris, Maintain good field sanitation, Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Tomato___Target_Spot.Treatment: Remove infected leaves at early stage, Improve field aeration and reduce leaf wetness, Apply recommended fungicides at proper intervals, Monitor disease regularly during warm and humid weather
Tomato___Target_Spot.Pesticide: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, Copper oxychloride, Carbendazim, Propiconazole, Azoxystrobin
Tomato___Target_Spot.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Trichoderma viride / Trichoderma harzianum, Garlic extract spray, Compost tea spray, Removal of infected plant parts

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.Cause:
Tomato mosaic disease is caused by a viral pathogen : Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV)
(Genus: Tobamovirus)
The virus is highly stable and spreads mainly through mechanical contact, contaminated tools, hands, clothing, seeds, and infected plant debris.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.Prevention: Use virus-free certified seeds and seedlings, Grow resistant or tolerant tomato varieties, Disinfect tools, hands, and equipment regularly, Avoid handling plants when they are wet, Remove and destroy infected plants immediately, Practice crop rotation, Control insect vectors that may aid spread, Avoid tobacco products while working in fields (virus can survive on tobacco)
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.Treatment: Rogue (remove) infected plants early, Maintain strict field sanitation, Prevent further spread through hygiene and vector control, Support plant health through balanced nutrition
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.Pesticide:
No pesticide can cure Tomato Mosaic Virus. However, chemicals are used to control vectors and secondary infections:
Vector control - Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam
Secondary fungal infection - Mancozeb, Copper oxychloride
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Milk spray (10%), Removal of infected plants, Tool disinfection using bleaching powder solution, Use of resistant varieties, Soil and crop hygiene

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.Cause:
Tomato yellow leaf curl disease is caused by a viral pathogen : Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
(Genus: Begomovirus, Family: Geminiviridae)
The virus is transmitted exclusively by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It is not seed-borne and does not spread through soil or water.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.Prevention: Use virus-free, healthy seedlings, Grow resistant or tolerant tomato varieties, Raise seedlings in insect-proof net houses, Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies, Remove and destroy infected plants immediately, Maintain field sanitation and weed control, Avoid overlapping tomato crops, Use reflective mulches to repel whiteflies
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.Treatment: Remove infected plants at early stage, Control whitefly population strictly, Follow integrated pest management practices, Maintain balanced fertilization to reduce plant stress
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.Pesticide:
Chemicals are used only to control whitefly vectors, not the virus itself:
Whitefly control - Imidacloprid
Whitefly control - Thiamethoxam
Whitefly control - Acetamiprid
Whitefly control - Spiromesifen
Whitefly control - Flonicamid
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.Organic solution: Neem oil spray (2–3%), Neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%), Yellow sticky traps, Reflective silver mulch, Removal of infected plants, Biological control agents
